common_name: Nikita Nerine (Pale Blush-Pink Hardy Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck sitting at or just above soil level in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; Nikita is a hardy bowdenii selection grown for its softer, paler flower color.

directions: Set bulbs with their necks at or barely above the soil surface in a warm, sheltered bed with sharp drainage, since standing moisture around the neck through winter is the main cause of loss in this cold-hardy Nerine bowdenii selection. Nikita sends up bare autumn stems carrying rounded heads of pale, blush-pink flowers with a faint darker flush toward the petal tips, a softer counterpart to the deeper pink of the wild species. Leave clumps undisturbed once established, since flowering builds steadily over several seasons and is reduced right after any division. A dry winter mulch over the dormant crown extends the hardy range toward the cooler edge of zone 7.

common_name: Zeal Salmon Nerine (Salmon-Pink Hardy Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or slightly above soil level in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; a Zeal Monachorum selection raised alongside the larger-flowered 'Zeal Giant'.

directions: Plant bulbs shallowly in a warm, south-facing border or against a wall where summer heat builds ahead of the autumn bloom, keeping the soil on the dry, lean side rather than rich and moisture-retentive. Zeal Salmon is one of several selections bred at Zeal Monachorum in Devon from the same breeding line as 'Zeal Giant', distinguished by its warmer salmon-pink tone rather than clear pink. Strap-shaped leaves emerge after the flower stems fade and persist through winter, so avoid cutting them back while still green. Established clumps resent disturbance and bloom most heavily when left to build size undivided for several years.

common_name: Conchiflora Tiger Flower (Cream and Crimson-Spotted Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F; a long-known pale, heavily spotted form of the species distinct from the solid-colored named forms.

directions: Plant bulbs three to four inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the ground has warmed thoroughly. Conchiflora carries pale cream to soft yellow outer petals densely freckled with crimson-maroon spotting toward the base, a heavily marked, shell-like pattern that gives the old varietal name its meaning and sets it apart from the cleaner solid tones of forms like 'Aurea' or 'Alba'. Each three-petaled flower lasts only a single day, but a well-fed clump keeps producing fresh blooms through most of the summer. Where winters drop below zone 8, lift the bulbs once frost blackens the foliage and store them dry and frost-free for replanting the following spring.

common_name: Rhode Island Red Pineapple Lily (Dark Burgundy-Black Foliage Pineapple Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; a Plant Delights Nursery selection prized for exceptionally dark, near-black foliage.

directions: Plant bulbs about four inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed in spring, choosing a full-sun spot that intensifies the foliage color rather than a shaded one that fades it toward green. Rhode Island Red, a Tony Avent introduction from Plant Delights Nursery, holds glossy, near-black-burgundy leaves from emergence through the summer flush of maroon-purple, star-shaped flowers topped by the pineapple-like leafy crown typical of the genus. Its dark coloring reads strongest against light gravel mulch or pale container glaze, so use those contrasts when siting it. Water regularly through active summer growth, taper off as the foliage yellows in fall, and protect the dormant bulb from hard freezes with mulch or by lifting where winters exceed its hardiness.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; a long-sold named color form popular in mixed Sparaxis bulb collections alongside 'Fire King'.

directions: Plant corms two to three inches deep in fall where winters stay mild, choosing well-drained, sandy soil in full sun so the summer dormancy stays dry. Jester carries an eye-catching mix of contrasting color bands radiating from a dark central blotch on each petal, a jumbled, harlequin-patterned bloom that gave the cultivar its name and makes it a popular component of mixed Sparaxis bulb collections. Group a generous number of corms together for impact, since the flowers are small individually, and let foliage die back fully before lifting corms in climates that require summer storage. In zones 8 through 10 the corms can stay in the ground year-round and will slowly naturalize.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free areas (zones 9-11) or start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost in cold climates; a classic RHS Award of Garden Merit white-flowered freesia.

directions: Plant corms about two inches deep and two to three inches apart in gritty, well-drained soil, since freesias rot readily in soggy ground, especially once flowering finishes. Alaska produces pure white, funnel-shaped single flowers with a light touch of cream in the throat, carried in loose spikes on wiry stems, and it remains one of the most widely grown fragrant white freesia cultivars decades after its introduction. Stake or grow the slender stems through twiggy support to keep the flower spikes from flopping as buds open. In frost-free gardens leave corms in the ground to multiply and naturalize; elsewhere lift after the foliage yellows, dry thoroughly, and store cool and dry until fall replanting.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies.

directions: Afterglow is a long-established Dutch corn lily hybrid producing warm salmon-orange, star-shaped flowers that deepen toward a small, glossy dark eye at the center of each bloom. Like other Ixia hybrids the wiry stems hold their flowers tightly closed on dull days, opening fully only under strong direct sun, so give this cultivar the sunniest, most sheltered spot in the border. Plant corms in bold clusters of twenty-five or more rather than scattering them singly, since the narrow grasslike foliage contributes little visual weight on its own. Let the foliage collapse and dry completely after bloom before lifting corms for summer storage in climates with humid or wet summers.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; a long-sold blue-violet selection that stands out from the mostly warm-toned Ixia hybrids.

directions: Bluebird is a classic named corn lily hybrid valued for its cool blue-violet coloring, a rare shade in a genus dominated by reds, oranges, pinks, and yellows, with each star-shaped flower marked by a small darker eye at the base of the segments. As with other Ixia cultivars, blooms held on the wiry stems stay closed in cloudy weather and open widest in full, direct sun, so reserve the brightest available bed for this selection. Planting corms in generous drifts of two dozen or more makes the color read as a distinct patch rather than disappearing among warmer-toned neighbors. Withhold water once foliage begins to yellow after bloom, and in areas with wet or humid summers lift and dry-store the corms until fall replanting.

common_name: Yellow Emperor Corn Lily (Golden-Yellow Ixia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; a long-cultivated solid golden-yellow Ixia hybrid.

directions: Yellow Emperor bears clear, solid golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers on wiry stems, a long-cultivated Dutch corn lily hybrid grown for its strong, uniform color rather than the contrasting eye seen in many other Ixia selections. Blooms remain closed on overcast days and open fully only in strong sun, so this cultivar performs best planted in the warmest, most exposed part of the bed. Set corms in bold drifts of two dozen or more for a solid sweep of color, since the narrow, grasslike foliage adds little bulk on its own. After bloom, let the foliage yellow and collapse fully before cutting back, and lift corms for dry summer storage wherever summers are humid or wet enough to risk rot during dormancy.
